It chiefly introduces conditions, but it can also flag an indirect question ("whether") or, paired with a negative, mean "except." In the Septuagint it shows up 646 times, usually standing in for the Hebrew word אם ("if"), 305 times. One interesting wrinkle from everyday Koine papyri: writers increasingly blurred the line between εἰ and the related word ἐάν, even occasionally pairing εἰ with verb forms it traditionally avoided.
prose.caution: Because εἰ is a grammatical particle rather than a content word, 116 of its 502 occurrences are absorbed into phrasing with no English word of their own, so the many short "sense" labels reflect translation patterns rather than distinct meanings.

prose.def: The Greek phrase meaning "you are" — the second person singular present of the verb "to be."
prose.article: This is simply the form of the Greek verb "to be" (εἰμί) that means "you are," addressed to one person. Like the English verb "to be," the parent verb covers existence, presence, identity, and what happens or takes place. Abbott-Smith lays out this wide range — from "to exist" (as in John 1:1) to "to be present" or "to come," and even impersonal uses like "there is."

It appears just 5 times in the Byzantine New Testament across 4 books, and notably is absent from the SBL critical text. Each of its occurrences is rendered slightly differently in the Majority Standard Bible—ranging from "surely" to "if you"—reflecting how the surrounding context shapes whether the condition feels assumed-true or genuinely open.

prose.def: A set phrase meaning "but if not" or "otherwise," introducing what would happen if a stated condition were not met.

It works like English "otherwise" or "or else," pointing to the alternative outcome if a condition is not met — and in the Byzantine New Testament it appears 8 times across 3 books. Interestingly, Abbott-Smith notes it follows both positive statements (Matthew 6:1, Luke 10:6) and negative ones (Matthew 9:17, Luke 5:36), so it can signal the flip side either way. The translation data shows it is most often rendered as part of a "will" clause (5 of 8 times), reflecting how English phrases the consequence rather than a one-word gloss.

prose.def: The outward appearance or visible form of something, or by extension its kind or sort.
prose.article: εἶδος means what something looks like — its outward appearance or shape — and from there it stretches to mean a kind or sort of thing. It appears 5 times in the New Testament, rendered "form" twice (50%), and once each as "form" (of God) and "sight" (in 2 Corinthians 5:7, where we walk by faith, not by sight). The Septuagint uses it 48 times, mostly for Hebrew words for appearance (מַרְאֶה) and figure or shape (תֹּאַר), and the papyri confirm the "kind" sense: business documents use the formula παντὸς εἴδους meaning "of every kind," which supports the rendering "every form of evil" in 1 Thessalonians 5:22.

prose.article: In the New Testament εἴδωλον almost always means an idol — either the physical image set up for worship or the false god behind it — rendered "idols" in 10 of its 11 occurrences (91%). prose.def: A form of the verb "to be" expressing what might, could, would, or should be — used for possibility rather than fact.
prose.article: εἴην is the present optative of εἰμί, the ordinary Greek verb "to be." Rather than stating that something simply is, this form softens the statement into what might, could, or would be the case. It does not appear in the Byzantine New Testament text at all, so the verb "to be" itself (εἰμί) covers the full range of meanings — existing, happening, being present, or the impersonal "there is." Moulton-Milligan confirms the word turns up in everyday Koine papyri and inscriptions, showing it was common in ordinary speech.
prose.caution: This optative form has zero occurrences in the Byzantine New Testament, so its meaning here rests entirely on the general usage of εἰμί and on outside evidence.
